style_method: Category pages for 11 women's clothing categories (T-Shirts, Tank Tops, Hoodies & Sweatshirts, Sweaters & Cardigans, Jackets & Vests, Blouses & Button-Up Shirts, Jeans, Pants & Sweatpants, Skirts, Shorts, Dresses & Jumpsuits). Each page serves only about 30 tiles, so tiles were read in three views per category (default, sale price ascending, sale price descending), giving 520 distinct style codes (style_colour collapsed to style). Composition read from the material field in the product page HTML, one page at a time. Lead fibre = highest share in the first composition listed; recycled polyester counted as polyester, recycled and organic cotton as cotton, TENCEL as lyocell, rayon as viscose, spandex as elastane.
sample_basis: 79 of 520 style codes reachable, stratified in proportion to the category counts the site states (sum 1,246 on 23 Oct 2026; categories overlap so this is not de-duplicated). The 520 are a biased window (featured plus cheapest and dearest tiles), so shares are indicative. One pyjama-set pant was dropped as sleepwear. All 79 sampled pages stated a composition.
fab_basis: Of 79: cotton leads 46 (58.2%); polyester 22 and polyamide 2, so synthetic leads 25 (31.6%); wool 1 (1.3%); linen 1 (1.3%); cashmere 0; silk 0; modal 2, viscose 2, lyocell 2 (cellulosic 7.6%). Denim read as denim cloth: 13 of 79 (16.5%), 12 jeans plus a denim shirt. Graphic tees and sweatshirts are cotton-heavy; knitwear, tanks, dresses and outerwear lean on recycled polyester.
tech_named_fabrics: Next Level Stretch (jeans), Dreamy Drape (denim), Rigid (denim label), Real Good (AE badge for its more sustainable items); lyocell or TENCEL(TM) fibres (Lenzing, licensed) in 9 of 79 sampled (3 labelled TENCEL); Soft & Sexy, Whoa So Soft, Hey Baby are fabric-feel names on knits
tech_owned_or_licensed: own marketing names for denim stretch and drape constructions (Next Level Stretch, Dreamy Drape); TENCEL is licensed from Lenzing; no owned patent or mill found
tech_share_of_range: Next Level Stretch or Dreamy Drape badges on 9 of the 33 jeans tiles read on the jeans page (5 Next Level Stretch, 4 Dreamy Drape) (jeans are 185 of 1,246 category items); lyocell or TENCEL in 9 of 79 sampled styles; not counted across the whole range
owned_facility: NONE (10-K for the year ended 31 Jan 2026: AEO designs and third-party factories manufacture; no owned factories; owns distribution centres)
named_makers: NONE (product pages say only "Imported"; the 10-K names no factories)
named_mills: NONE on product pages (Lenzing named as TENCEL fibre supplier only; no denim or fabric mill named on the 79 pages)
made_in_stated_share: 0% (79 of 79 sampled pages say "Imported"; no country stated)
heritage_claim: dated and placed for the company: first AE store opened 1977 in Twelve Oaks Mall, Novi, Michigan (AEO timeline); nothing on where garments are made
process_documented: no (ae.com and the 10-K describe fits, stretch and sustainability badges, not how garments are made)
craft_reasoning: AEO states in its 10-K that it owns no factories and third parties make everything. All 79 sampled product pages say only "Imported", with no country, factory or mill. The only dated, placed claim is the 1977 first store in Novi, Michigan, which is retail history, not making. Nothing checkable about who makes the clothes, so a 1.
note: Part 1 dials read 22-23 Oct 2026 from ae.com US. Own label only: AE and AE77 Premium (AE77 is AE's own upper line, 14 of 79 sampled). Aerie is a separate brand and not read. AE also sells men's: women's category pages only; unisex pieces not seen in the sample. Sleepwear excluded (one pyjama-set pant dropped), swim not sampled. Status partial: the 520-style window is biased toward featured and price extremes and the site total is not de-duplicated. Shoes sold include outside brands (Ariat, Dr. Martens, Timberland), not clothing and not sampled.
